args.text:
Listen, there's no such thing as a safe spot outside when there's thunderstorms about. None. Not under a tree, not out on the paddock, nowhere. If ya can hear thunder, chances are yer already within strikin' distance of the bloody thing. So just remember the line, “When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!” Trouble is, too many people leave it way too late to get somewhere safe when a storm's rollin' in, and sadly, that dawdlin' is behind a lot of the lightnin' deaths and injuries in the U.S.

Best way to look after yerself with lightnin'? Don't be anywhere near it. Simple as that. Ya do not wanna get caught out in a storm. So have a lightnin' safety plan, and if thunderstorms are forecast, pull the pin on the footy or the barbie or whatever it is, or put it off, and do it early. Keep an eye on the weather and get yerself somewhere safe before it turns nasty. A solid building's a safe bet, and so's a car with a proper hard roof. A rain shelter, a little shed, an open vehicle? No good. Not safe, any of 'em.

Now, once yer inside, it's not over. Don't touch anythin' plugged into a power point, don't touch the plumbin', and don't touch a phone with a cord on it. Yer mobile's fine, and so's a cordless phone. Keep away from outside doors and windows too, and whatever ya do, don't go lyin' on the garage floor.

Gettin' Yer Head Round the Threat

Here's the thing. Whether someone cops a lightnin' strike comes down to how they carry on when thunderstorms are about. The graphs below give ya a squiz at why people get struck, when they get struck, and what they can do to cut their odds.

Take the first graph. The threat of lightnin' climbs as a thunderstorm rolls in, hits its peak when the storm's sittin' right over yer head, then slowly tapers off as it moves away. But here's the kicker: it's how people carry on that decides the risk of a strike that kills ya. Some head inside at the first sign of a storm. Good on 'em. Heaps of others leave it way too late. Some hang about till the thing's right overhead and the rain's bucketin' down. Others never planned for it, so they get caught outside with nowhere safe to get to. Most people do make it inside, fair enough, but then some go and put themselves at risk anyway, touchin' things that can get electrified if lightnin' hits nearby. And last of all, heaps of people wander back out too soon after the storm looks to have cleared off, often only waitin' till the rain eases or stops. Every one of those habits, the whole lot of 'em, is what puts people at risk when thunderstorms are about.

Cuttin' the Risk

So how d'ya keep yer own risk of gettin' hit as low as it'll go? When ya head outside, plan ahead, so ya can get somewhere safe quick smart if a thunderstorm's brewin'. If the sky's turnin' nasty or ya hear thunder, get inside somewhere safe. Straight away, not after one more over. Once yer in, keep off phones with a cord, electrical gear and the plumbin', and keep away from the windows and doors. Then wait 30 minutes after the last lightnin' or the last rumble of thunder before ya head back out. Thirty minutes. If every bloke and sheila stuck to those few simple rules, we'd see a lot fewer lightnin' casualties in this country.

So remember, it's how you carry on when thunderstorms are about that decides yer own risk of gettin' struck. When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!

Lightnin' Victims

And if someone does get struck by lightnin', they might need medical help straight away. Now, this bit's important: a lightnin' victim doesn't carry an electrical charge, so they're safe to touch. Don't stand there. Call 911 and keep an eye on 'em. Start CPR or use an Automated External Defibrillator if needed.
